title: How the Web Works
description: Build the foundational mental model of the web: browsers send HTTP requests across the network, servers process and respond with status codes and resources, and the browser orchestrates rendering.

objectives.statement: Explain the request/response cycle between a browser and a server across the network.
Distinguish between client request parameters and server response headers/bodies.

content.title: The Conversation of the Web
content.hook: When you visit a website, your computer is not opening a local file on your hard drive — it is holding a live conversation with a remote computer.
content.context: Every single page view, button click, search query, and image load involves a browser sending a request across the internet and a server returning a response. Understanding this conversation is what separates frontend engineers from people who just write HTML files on their desktop.
goals: Distinguish request data (method, URL, headers) from response data (status code, body).
Trace why loading a webpage requires networked communication.

content.title: The Request / Response Exchange
content.description: The browser acts as the client: it formulates an HTTP Request (e.g. GET /dashboard). The server processes the request and sends back an HTTP Response containing a status code (e.g. 200 OK) and a payload (HTML, JSON, CSS, images).

content.prompt: Suppose a user navigates to `https://example.com/profile`. Which option accurately describes the exchange between the browser and server?
options: The browser opens the profile file from local storage without contacting any network server.
The browser sends an HTTP GET request to example.com; the server verifies the route and returns an HTTP 200 response with the profile HTML.
The server commands the browser's hardware to execute SQL database queries directly on the client machine.
The browser executes the entire backend database query locally in memory before informing the server.

validation.expected: The browser sends an HTTP GET request to example.com; the server verifies the route and returns an HTTP 200 response with the profile HTML.

feedback.correct: Correct! The browser formulates and dispatches an HTTP GET request; the remote server processes it, accesses any necessary database state, and responds with status 200 OK and HTML payload.
feedback.incorrect: Remember the client-server boundary: the browser requests resources over the network; the remote server processes data and returns a response.

content.question: Which of the following are components created by and returned in an HTTP Response from a web server? (Select all that apply)

options.text: HTTP Status Code (e.g. 200 OK, 404 Not Found)
Response Body (e.g. HTML document, JSON payload)
User-Agent Header sent by browser describing browser version

feedback.correct: Spot on! The server returns status codes, response headers, and the response body. User-Agent is sent by the client in the Request.
feedback.incorrect: Review which side produces each header: the client sends User-Agent in the request, while the server returns status codes, Content-Type headers, and response bodies.

content.prompt: In your own words, explain why viewing a live website is fundamentally different from opening a `.html` file saved locally on your laptop's hard drive. Mention the roles of request and response.

feedback.correct: Great articulation! A live website relies on networked HTTP request/response conversations across distributed computers, whereas local files bypass network communication entirely.
feedback.incorrect: Ensure your explanation discusses the network communication boundary between client and server.

content.title: Key Takeaways: Web Communication
takeaways: The web operates on a client-server architecture powered by HTTP request/response exchanges.
Clients (browsers) request resources using methods like GET and POST with target URLs.
Servers process requests and return responses containing status codes (200, 404, 500), headers, and data payloads.
Frontend development takes place on the client side, interpreting the server's response to construct the interactive UI.
